description: Live view of what the market-data collectors are writing into the shared `dropset` database. Read the rows top-down, quotability first: Can I quote right now is the go/no-go verdict, Are the feeds alive says which collectors and sources are behind it, and Does the price look right is the shape read. Collapse the rows you are not using — a bring-up reader wants the middle one, a live-quoting reader wants the top one. The refresh is 30s: the tightest bound anything here renders is the 300-second store-silence bound, and the default range is two days, so a 5-second refresh re-ran every windowed query 192 times more work than it had before for no extra signal.

links.title: Halt state and the estimator
links.tooltip: The maker side of the go/no-go reading: whether the engine is actually halted, and whether the fair it quotes off is defensible against the prints it was built from. This dashboard says whether the DATA supports a quote; that one says what the maker did about it. Deliberately not variable-carrying, since a market and an FX product id are different vocabularies.

links.title: Cross-pair index
links.tooltip: Of every pair carrying a currency, which moved most and when — the per-symbol reading, which lives on the FX analytics dashboard as the Cross-pair index panel. Linked because the acceptance condition it discharges is a walkthrough condition and must not require knowing which of two dashboards to open.

links.title: All data
links.tooltip: Widen the time range to start at the candlestick selection's own first collected bar, keeping the current pickers. Exists because the time picker's presets are all relative to now and none of them can know when collection actually started. Drag-selecting on a chart zooms in and there is no equally obvious way back out, so this is the way back out.

links.title: Last 24h
links.tooltip: Narrow to the last day, keeping the current pickers. At 60s buckets this is the widest window where individual candles are still readable.

panels.description:
CAN WE QUOTE RIGHT NOW. One live trusted tape is the criterion and the halt is at zero, so the OANDA tape column is the only one that decides anything — everything beside it is context for diagnosing why.

OANDA is the designated tape: the anchor treated as truth. That is a DESIGNATION, not a measurement, and no column in the store records it. Twelve Data carries the same pairs intraday and is deliberately not believable alone, which is exactly why the two are never pooled into one count — one-live-of-two says nothing until you know which one. A daily reference can never reach this column, so it can never clear the halt.

TAPE AGE IS THE MAGNITUDE BEHIND THE VERDICT. The freshness picker is the halt's detection latency rather than a display preference; the OANDA tape column is the pass/fail against it, and this column is how far past it the tape has actually gone. Deliberately NOT color-coded, for a reason worth knowing: Grafana cannot interpolate a template variable into a threshold, so any fixed bound here would disagree with the verdict column at every picker setting except one — and a raw-seconds column is uncolored everywhere else on this dashboard. It is what separates "quiet for a minute" from "quiet since Friday". Expect it to sit red across an FX weekend: the tape stops at the Friday close by design, so a no-go on every FX pair from Friday evening to Sunday is CORRECT rather than an incident, The FX analytics dashboard carries a weekend annotation on its time-series panels; this dashboard has none, so the tape-age column is the whole of the context here.

Stale (was live) is where an outage lands FIRST, and it is a transition bucket rather than a cumulative one: past the class bound a source leaves the live population entirely, so the count rises and then falls back. Read it against Printing now to tell an outage from an ordinary cadence. Corroborating counts any fresh non-tape source, so a daily reference lands there for the freshness window after it publishes — which is why it is context and never a criterion.

THE LONG TAIL IS WITHHELD, counted in the final row. Pairs with no live trusted tape were thirty-odd rows reading zero in the only column that decides anything, whose effect was to teach the eye to skip the table. Note a withheld pair may still have live sources — every crypto and peg leg does, since only OANDA is ever the trusted tape — the same reason the constant Pyth column was removed. Source coverage below gives every source by name, including the parked one, which is where thin-roster visibility belongs.

targets.rawSql:
-- Can we quote right now. THE CRITERION IS ONE LIVE TRUSTED TAPE, halt at
-- zero -- ruled by the operator on 2026-09-10, replacing a "survives one or
-- two venues dark" reading that could not be implemented because it
-- contradicted itself. So the tape column is the only one that decides
-- anything; everything beside it is context.
--
-- The trusted tape is oanda, named here as a literal because primacy is a
-- DESIGNATION rather than a measurement -- it is the anchor treated as truth,
-- and no column in the store records that. Twelve Data carries the same pairs
-- intraday and is deliberately not believable alone, which is precisely why
-- the two must not be pooled into one count: one-live-of-two says nothing
-- until you know which one.
--
-- TAPE AGE IS THE HALT BOUND MADE READABLE, and it is the reading this panel
-- previously left implicit. The freshness picker IS the halt's detection
-- latency, so showing the tape's actual age beside the verdict is what lets a
-- reader see how far past the bound the tape has gone rather than only that it
-- failed. It is also the one column that distinguishes "quiet for a minute"
-- from "quiet since Friday" without a second panel.
--
-- WHY THERE IS NO CADENCE CLASSIFIER HERE, since the obvious way to write
-- this panel has one and it is a trap. An earlier version split sources into
-- intraday and daily by counting readings in a six-hour window, which fails
-- in the worst possible direction: a genuinely intraday venue that has been
-- down for more than six hours has no readings in the window, so it stops
-- counting as intraday and lands in the daily population -- while
-- instrument_source_liveness still reports it live, because that bound is 48
-- to 72 hours. A long outage therefore made the panel look HEALTHIER. Verified
-- against the store: a source can be is_live with zero readings in six hours.
--
-- Freshness alone does the work instead, and under the ruled criterion that
-- is sufficient rather than a compromise: cadence only ever mattered as a
-- proxy for "could this price a quote right now", and a designated tape plus
-- a recency test answers that directly, fail-closed.
--
-- THE LONG TAIL IS CUT to the anchors plus any pair with a live tape, with the
-- remainder counted in a final row. Those rows all read tape_live = 0, which on
-- a non-anchor pair is thirty-odd rows the reader must learn to ignore -- the
-- same defect that removed the constant dark column: a value that never varies
-- costs width and teaches the eye to skip the table. Be precise about what the
-- cut removes, because the obvious phrasing overstates it: a withheld pair may
-- well have live sources (every crypto and peg leg does, since `trusted` can
-- only ever be oanda), so the footer says "no live trusted tape" and not "no
-- live source". Source coverage below delivers by-name visibility for every
-- thin-roster currency, which is where a reader goes for those.
--
-- WHY `is_live` IS NOT CONJOINED WITH `fresh` in the three filters below. It
-- would be dead: the view's bound is 48 to 72 hours and `fresh` is minutes, so
-- `fresh` strictly implies `is_live` (confirmed against the store -- zero rows
-- are fresh without being live). Carrying it anyway would only invite the
-- reader to think this panel treats `is_live` as a quoting signal, which is
-- exactly the reading the spec rules out. It IS load-bearing in
-- stale_was_live, where the pair `is_live AND NOT fresh` is the transition
-- bucket itself.
--
-- THE MVP ANCHORS ARE A LITERAL, which is deliberate. There is no legitimate
-- state in which an MVP anchor is absent, so this panel has to be unable to
-- lose one. A de-rostered product leaves the registry, so a purely
-- registry-driven read would drop it silently -- the same
-- invisible-rather-than-dark defect the coverage panel exists to catch.
WITH anchor AS (
  SELECT a.product_id
  FROM (VALUES
    ('EUR-USD'),
    ('AUD-USD'),
    ('CAD-USD')
  ) AS a (product_id)
),

scope AS (
  SELECT a.product_id FROM anchor AS a
  UNION
  SELECT l.product_id FROM instrument_source_liveness AS l
),

graded AS (
  SELECT
    s.product_id,
    l.source,
    l.is_live,
    l.last_data_at,
    extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_data_at
      <= ${quote_freshness_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60 AS fresh,
    -- COUPLED to the exact source spelling the collectors register. The feeds
    -- framework names some sources per product (a venue can register as
    -- `venue:PRODUCT`), so if oanda ever adopted that shape this equality
    -- would stop matching and every pair would read no-go. That fails CLOSED
    -- -- a permanent false halt, loud rather than silent, and diagnosable
    -- because the venue still appears in printing_now -- which is why it is
    -- left as a plain equality rather than a prefix match that could also
    -- match a different venue whose name merely starts the same way.
    l.source = 'oanda' AS trusted
  FROM scope AS s
  LEFT JOIN instrument_source_liveness AS l ON l.product_id = s.product_id
),

per_pair AS (
  SELECT
    g.product_id,
    EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM anchor AS a WHERE a.product_id = g.product_id)
      AS is_anchor,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.trusted AND g.fresh) AS tape_live,
    max(g.last_data_at) FILTER (WHERE g.trusted) AS tape_last_at,
    -- One honest edge, visible rather than hidden: a daily reference counts
    -- here for the freshness window after it publishes, so this column can
    -- briefly read 1 on an FX pair whose only intraday tape is dead. That is
    -- why it is context and never a criterion -- it can never reach tape_live,
    -- so it can never clear the halt, which is what the ruling requires of a
    -- daily reference. Read it against printing_now, which names the source.
    count(*) FILTER (
      WHERE NOT g.trusted AND g.fresh
    ) AS corroborating,
    -- Where an outage lands FIRST, which is not where it stays: past the class
    -- bound the source drops out of is_live entirely, so this counter rises
    -- and then falls back. It is a TRANSITION bucket, not a cumulative one.
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.is_live AND NOT g.fresh) AS stale_was_live,
    string_agg(g.source, ', ' ORDER BY g.source) FILTER (
      WHERE g.fresh
    ) AS printing_now
  FROM graded AS g
  GROUP BY g.product_id
),

shown AS (
  SELECT p.* FROM per_pair AS p WHERE p.is_anchor OR p.tape_live > 0
),

withheld AS (
  SELECT count(*) AS n
  FROM per_pair AS p
  WHERE NOT (p.is_anchor OR p.tape_live > 0)
)

SELECT
  0 AS sort_group,
  s.product_id,
  s.tape_live,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - s.tape_last_at)::bigint AS tape_age_secs,
  s.corroborating,
  s.stale_was_live,
  s.printing_now
FROM shown AS s
UNION ALL
SELECT
  1 AS sort_group,
  w.n || ' further pairs withheld: no live trusted tape'
    AS product_id,
  NULL AS tape_live,
  NULL AS tape_age_secs,
  NULL AS corroborating,
  NULL AS stale_was_live,
  NULL AS printing_now
FROM withheld AS w
WHERE w.n > 0
ORDER BY 1 ASC, 3 ASC, 2 ASC

panels.title: Live venues per pair

panels.description:
Is every cursor-based collector process alive and committing right now, in wall-clock seconds. FOURTEEN ROWS EXPECTED — one per cursor-capable (source, product) in the registry.

This is the only true wall-clock liveness signal in the schema, and it answers a different question from the coverage tables beside and below it. Those measure when DATA last arrived, which a closed venue suppresses even while the collector is healthy. Measured after the Friday FX close: OANDA's cursor was 33 seconds old while its newest candle was two hours old. The collector was fine; the market was shut.

AGE IS COUNTED IN EXPECTED COMMITS, not seconds, which is what lets one bound serve a 60-second poller and a once-a-day collector at the same time. The 300-second store-silence bound this panel carries is five commits for a 60s source, so orange at 3 and red at 5 carries it over (to within the one-decimal rounding, which trips red at 297s) — while a daily collector, which is 86400 seconds old whenever it is perfectly healthy, now reads about 1.0 instead of permanently red. Age in seconds is kept beside it as raw context and is not colored.

A row reading NO CURSOR is a (source, product) the registry knows about for which no cursor has ever been committed. That is what this table's shape buys: the roster comes from the registry, so a cursor that disappears leaves a row behind rather than an absent tile.

ONLY PAGED COLLECTORS APPEAR HERE, deliberately. Kraken, er-api and Frankfurter are HTTP live sources that never commit a cursor, and Pyth is parked, so rows for them could never populate — an unscoped registry join renders 73 rows of which 59 are permanently empty. Source coverage is the panel that accounts for all eight sources by name.

targets.rawSql:
-- Is every cursor-based collector process alive and committing right now, in
-- wall clock. This is the only true wall-clock liveness signal in the schema:
-- every other freshness reading measures when DATA last arrived, which a
-- closed venue suppresses even while the collector is perfectly healthy.
-- Measured instance of exactly that: after the Friday FX close oanda's cursor
-- was 33 seconds old while its newest candle was two hours old. Reading the
-- two as one number would have reported a collector outage that was not
-- happening.
--
-- SCOPED TO THE CURSOR-CAPABLE SOURCES, which is a deliberate narrowing of
-- the registry rather than a plain registry read. Only paged collectors commit
-- a cursor; kraken, erapi and frankfurter are HTTP live sources that must not
-- adopt Backfill at all, and pyth is parked, so a cursor for any of them
-- cannot exist. Joining the whole registry renders 73 rows of which 59 are
-- permanently empty -- strictly worse than the tile wall this replaces, and
-- the same "rows the reader learns to ignore" defect that cut the per-pair
-- long tail. Registry-driven WITHIN that scope still buys the property that
-- matters: a cursor row that disappears leaves its (source, product) behind as
-- a row, so an absence renders rather than vanishing.
--
-- AGE IS COUNTED IN EXPECTED COMMITS, not seconds, and that is what lets one
-- bound serve every source. The 300-second store-silence bound this panel
-- carries was written for the 60-second pollers, where it is five commits; a
-- daily collector is 86400 seconds old whenever it is perfectly healthy, so the
-- same absolute bound painted four alphavantage rows permanently red. Orange
-- at 3 and red at 5 carries the 300s bound over to a 60s source -- within the
-- rounding, which is one decimal, so red actually trips at 297s rather than at
-- 300s exactly -- while reading correctly for a daily one.
WITH expected AS (
  SELECT
    r.source,
    r.product_id,
    d.expected_secs
  FROM instrument_registry AS r
  INNER JOIN (VALUES
    ('oanda', 60),
    ('twelvedata', 60),
    ('coinbase', 60),
    ('alphavantage', 86400)
  ) AS d (source, expected_secs) ON r.source = d.source
)

SELECT
  e.source,
  e.product_id,
  (extract(epoch FROM now() - fc.updated_at))::bigint AS age_secs,
  round(
    extract(epoch FROM now() - fc.updated_at) / e.expected_secs, 1
  ) AS age_commits
FROM expected AS e
LEFT JOIN feed_cursors AS fc
  ON
    split_part(fc.feed, ':', 2) = e.source
    AND split_part(fc.feed, ':', 3) = e.product_id
ORDER BY
  age_commits DESC NULLS FIRST,
  e.source ASC,
  e.product_id ASC

panels.title: Collector cursor age (wall clock)

panels.description:
Is every source the platform is meant to have contributing anywhere — including one that has produced nothing at all. AT LEAST EIGHT ROWS: the roster is declared — seven sources expected to be running plus Pyth, which is parked — so a source cannot answer this question by being absent from it, and a further row appears if the registry ever holds a source nobody declared. Rows are ordered by role rather than alphabetically, so the designated tapes sit at the top and the sources that are quiet by design sit at the bottom. If you are asking "are we getting data from Kraken, or Frankfurter, or er-api?", this is the panel that answers it, by name.

READ Printing now, NOT Covered. Covered is a 48-to-72-hour class-aware bound that answers "should this source be producing at all" and deliberately tolerates an FX weekend — it was measured reading true at 24.6 hours old, so it is not a quoting signal and never was. Printing now applies the tape freshness bound and fails closed.

A daily reference reads 0 under Printing now BETWEEN PUBLICATIONS, and that is correct rather than a fault — the Role column is what tells you which sources those are. This is also why there is no longer a single column called live: five covered sources on an FX pair is not five-fold redundancy, because three of them are daily references and only two quote intraday.

Role is a DESIGNATION, not a measurement, and is declared in this query as a literal. Nothing in the store records whether a source is a tape or a reference, and every version that derived it from the readings was suppressed by the outages it needed to report. The cost is drift when the roster changes, which is why a source nobody declared renders as UNCLASSIFIED instead of quietly joining a group. Panel Price by source carries the same designation in its line styling and the two must be kept in step; the durable fix is a collector-written cadence column in the registry.

PARKED IS NOT FAULTED, and this table now says which is which by joining rather than by pointing at prose. A source parked by decision reads role 'parked by decision' with the date in Parked since, both mirrored from the code constant that decides it (PARKED_SOURCES in feeds/src/parked.rs) into reference data at collector startup. Pyth is the parked one. Zeros on a parked row are correct and expected: nothing is running to produce, which is the whole point.

A DECLARED SOURCE READING UNCLASSIFIED IS THE LOUD CASE, and it now has a second cause worth knowing. It means either the registry holds a source nobody declared, or a declared source's park has not been confirmed by the mirror — which is what you see on a database no collector has started against, since the mirror is written at collector startup. Either way the row sorts first because nothing accounts for it.

WHAT A PARKED ROW STILL CANNOT TELL YOU, since a mirror is not an observation. The rows say what the last-started collector's build believed, so a park decided since then is real in code and not yet here — Park confirmed is when this park state was last written, and it is the only thing on this page that says so. A parked venue whose container was started ANYWAY is the quiet fault §4 of docs/dashboards.md calls the worst thing this page can render, and no panel here is built to catch it: the one tell is this row's own counts, since a running collector registers products and prints, so a parked row with non-zero Products or Printing now is a started-anyway venue. Do not look to Collector cursor age for it — that panel joins a four-source literal Pyth is not in, and a latest-price feed writes no cursor even when healthy. The reason a source is parked is not a column, deliberately — it is prose too long for a cell; read it beside the decision in the constant.

targets.rawSql:
-- Every source the collectors REGISTERED, whether or not it is producing, and
-- the DESIGNATED role that says how to read its counts.
--
-- The two coverage tables below group over a measurement table, so a source
-- that wrote nothing has no rows to group and vanishes entirely; absence there
-- cannot be told apart from never having been configured. Driving from the
-- registry inverts that, and a dark collector becomes a row reading 0 rather
-- than a row that is not there.
--
-- THE ROSTER IS A DECLARED LITERAL of EIGHT sources -- seven the platform
-- expects to be RUNNING plus the parked one -- so this table has an
-- unconditional FLOOR of eight rows. What the mirror below supplies is the park
-- STATE (the role text and the two dates), never the row itself: a row sourced
-- from the mirror alone would vanish on any database no collector has started
-- against. A further row appears if the
-- registry ever holds a source nobody declared, which is the loud case below. A registry-only
-- read cannot promise that, because a source leaves the registry when its
-- collector stops registering -- exactly the invisible-rather-than-dark defect
-- one level up that this panel exists to catch. The full join is what makes it
-- fail closed in both directions: a declared source missing from the registry
-- still renders as a row of zeros, and a source in the registry that nobody
-- declared renders with role UNCLASSIFIED rather than blending in.
--
-- WHY ROLE IS A LITERAL AND NOT DERIVED. Whether a source is a designated tape
-- or a daily reference is a DESIGNATION, and no column in the store records
-- it. Every derivable form is the shape this run deleted: any cadence measured
-- from the readings themselves is suppressed by the very outage it must
-- report. A literal cannot be suppressed, at the cost of drifting when the
-- roster changes -- which is why an undeclared source is loud. The durable fix
-- is a collector-written cadence column in the registry, filed as a gap.
--
-- READ printing_now, NOT covered. covered is the view's class-aware bound, 48
-- to 72 hours, which answers "should this source be producing at all" and
-- tolerates an FX weekend; it was measured returning true at 24.6 hours old,
-- so it must never be read as a quoting signal. printing_now applies the tape
-- freshness bound instead and is the fail-closed reading. A daily reference
-- shows 0 there between publications BY DESIGN, and its role column is what
-- says so -- which is also why the two counts are no longer one column called
-- live, a name that invited reading five sources as five-fold redundancy when
-- the real intraday redundancy on an FX pair is two.
WITH declared AS (
  SELECT
    d.source,
    d.role
  FROM (VALUES
    ('oanda', 'tape (FX)'),
    ('twelvedata', 'intraday margin (FX)'),
    ('coinbase', 'tape (crypto/peg)'),
    ('kraken', 'tape (crypto/peg)'),
    ('alphavantage', 'daily reference'),
    ('erapi', 'daily reference'),
    ('frankfurter', 'daily reference'),
    -- PYTH STAYS IN THE ROSTER WITH A NULL ROLE, and both halves of that are
    -- load-bearing. It stays because the roster is what gives this table its
    -- FLOOR: sourcing a parked source's row from the mirror alone would make
    -- it VANISH on any database no collector has started against -- rendering
    -- as never-configured, which is the invisible-rather-than-dark defect this
    -- panel exists to catch, reintroduced by the fix for it. Its role is NULL
    -- because a designation is not what the roster knows about a parked source
    -- and 'parked by decision' is not a designation: the park state comes from
    -- the mirror below, so this literal holds no copy of the parked list. A
    -- parked source whose mirror row is missing therefore reads UNCLASSIFIED
    -- and sorts FIRST -- loud, which is the correct reading of "declared, dark,
    -- and nothing can tell me why".
    ('pyth', NULL)
  ) AS d (source, role)
),

-- THE PARK STATE, JOINED RATHER THAN COPIED. The literal above used to give
-- pyth the role 'parked by decision', which made this query hold its own copy
-- of a decision that lives in `feeds/src/parked.rs` -- the exact copy-drift the
-- declared roster exists to kill, one level in. Now the literal names the
-- source with a NULL role and the mirror says whether it is parked, so the
-- park state has one home. Be precise about what that does and does not
-- remove: the roster still names pyth, so un-parking it for good still means
-- editing this literal -- but forgetting to costs a loud UNCLASSIFIED row
-- rather than a stale claim that it is parked.
--
-- `mirrored_at` IS selected and IS shown, under a name that says what it dates.
-- It dates the last COLLECTOR START rather than the park, so the risk is that a
-- reader takes it for a data-freshness signal -- but withholding it costs more
-- than that risk: a stale mirror is the one failure mode of this whole design,
-- and if no surface renders the column then "mirrored_at makes staleness
-- legible" is a claim with nothing behind it.
parked AS (
  SELECT
    p.venue AS source,
    p.since,
    p.mirrored_at
  FROM parked_sources AS p
),

rolled AS (
  SELECT
    l.source,
    count(*) AS products,
    count(l.last_data_at) AS ever_produced,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE l.is_live) AS covered,
    count(*) FILTER (
      WHERE
        extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_data_at
        <= ${quote_freshness_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60
    ) AS printing_now,
    max(l.last_data_at) AS latest
  FROM instrument_source_liveness AS l
  GROUP BY l.source
)

SELECT
  coalesce(r.source, d.source, k.source) AS source,
  -- PARKED-NESS WINS OVER A DECLARED ROLE, and the order of these arms is the
  -- whole of that. Coalescing `d.role` first would mean a source that is BOTH
  -- declared and parked renders under its old designation with zero counts --
  -- i.e. as a faulted tape -- which is exactly the confusion this panel is
  -- meant to end, and it is the state a park transition passes through.
  CASE
    WHEN k.source IS NOT NULL THEN 'parked by decision'
    ELSE coalesce(d.role, 'UNCLASSIFIED')
  END AS role,
  k.since AS parked_since,
  -- THE MIRROR'S OWN AGE, shown rather than withheld. A parked row is only as
  -- current as the last collector start, so a mirror that has fallen behind the
  -- code constant is a real state -- and every other statement about this set
  -- calls `mirrored_at` the thing that makes that legible, which is only true if
  -- something renders it. Nothing else does: no other panel reads it and no
  -- alert rule watches it. Read it as "when was this park state last
  -- confirmed", never as a data-freshness signal for the source itself, which
  -- is what `latest` and `age_secs` are for.
  to_timestamp(k.mirrored_at) AS park_confirmed,
  coalesce(r.products, 0) AS products,
  coalesce(r.ever_produced, 0) AS ever_produced,
  coalesce(r.printing_now, 0) AS printing_now,
  coalesce(r.covered, 0) AS covered,
  to_timestamp(r.latest) AS latest,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - r.latest)::bigint AS age_secs
FROM rolled AS r
FULL JOIN declared AS d ON r.source = d.source
-- A THIRD FULL JOIN, for the same fail-closed reason as the second. A parked
-- source is in neither the registry nor the declared roster -- that is what
-- being parked means -- so an inner or left join would drop its row and this
-- panel would go back to being unable to say the word. Joining on the coalesce
-- of the two sides above is what lets a source that is BOTH declared and parked
-- still match one row rather than two.
FULL JOIN parked AS k ON coalesce(r.source, d.source) = k.source
-- ORDERED BY ROLE RANK, not alphabetically. Alphabetical put the three daily
-- references at the TOP -- and they read 0 under printing_now between
-- publications, so the first three rows of the table were permanently red while
-- the designated tape sat near the bottom. That is precisely the
-- teach-the-eye-to-skip-the-table defect cited twice above. An undeclared source
-- ranks first because it is the one thing here nobody has accounted for.
-- RANKED IN THE SAME PRECEDENCE THE ROLE COLUMN USES, parked first-tested and
-- sorted last, so the two agree about which tier a row is in. They agree on
-- PARKED-NESS specifically; a declared role added to the literal without a rank
-- arm below still falls to the terminal ELSE and sorts among the parked, which
-- is the pre-existing shape of this CASE rather than something the park state
-- introduced. An
-- UNCLASSIFIED row still ranks first because it is the one thing here nobody
-- has accounted for -- which now includes a DECLARED source whose park the
-- mirror has not confirmed, and that is the loud reading it should get.
ORDER BY
  CASE
    WHEN k.source IS NOT NULL THEN 5
    WHEN d.role IS NULL THEN 0
    WHEN d.role = 'tape (FX)' THEN 1
    WHEN d.role = 'intraday margin (FX)' THEN 2
    WHEN d.role = 'tape (crypto/peg)' THEN 3
    WHEN d.role = 'daily reference' THEN 4
    ELSE 5
  END ASC,
  coalesce(r.source, d.source, k.source) ASC

panels.title: Source coverage (every declared source)

panels.description:
Which sources cover which products in the candle tier, how much history each holds, and how fresh each is. The store-inventory definition for both dashboards.

Every (source, product, bucket width) the store has EVER held is a row, so a series that stopped entirely stays visible instead of dropping out of a window. Read three columns together: Bars (all time) is how much history exists, Buckets in window is whether it is still arriving, and Age (buckets) is how late it is. All-time bars with zero in-window buckets is a series that STOPPED — the one reading no windowed panel can give you.

AGE IS COUNTED IN BUCKETS, NOT SECONDS, and that is why the buckets column is the colored one. A daily series is 86400 seconds old just before its next bar lands, so an absolute bound tuned for 60s bars marks a perfectly healthy daily reference red forever. Dividing by the series' own bucket width makes one bound correct for both: about 1 is current, 2 is the bar in progress, orange at 4 and red at 8. Age in seconds is kept beside it as raw context and is deliberately not colored.

The window is independent of the dashboard time range on purpose: what is arriving now should not change when you pan back to look at history.

targets.rawSql:
-- The candle tier's store inventory and its freshness in one definition,
-- absorbing what the old Last candle age tile and the FX dashboard's What is
-- in the store table each answered on their own.
--
-- DRIVEN FROM ALL TIME, windowed only in a column. A series that stopped
-- entirely has no rows inside any window, so a windowed GROUP BY drops it and
-- the reader cannot tell "stopped" from "never configured" -- that reading is
-- what the FX table contributed and it has to survive the merge. Here every
-- (source, product, bucket width) the store has ever held is a row, and
-- buckets_in_window falling to 0 is what says it stopped.
--
-- STALENESS IS CADENCE-RELATIVE, which is why age_secs is not the colored
-- column. A daily series is 86400 seconds old the moment before its next
-- bucket lands, so any absolute bound correct for 60s bars paints a healthy
-- daily reference permanently red -- the defect that made the FX table's
-- 300/3600 thresholds wrong rather than merely noisy, measured on a source
-- whose bars are 86400s wide. age_cadences divides by the series' own bucket
-- width, so one number reads correctly for both: about 1 is current, 2 is the
-- bucket in progress, and the colored bounds sit at 4 and 8 so a weekend of a
-- daily reference does not read like an outage.
WITH lifetime AS (
  SELECT
    c.source,
    c.product_id,
    c.granularity_secs,
    count(*) AS bars_all_time,
    max(c.bucket_start) AS last_bucket
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
),

windowed AS (
  SELECT
    c.source,
    c.product_id,
    c.granularity_secs,
    count(*) AS buckets
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  WHERE c.bucket_start
    >= extract(epoch FROM now()) - (${coverage_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60)
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)

SELECT
  l.source,
  l.product_id,
  l.granularity_secs,
  l.bars_all_time,
  coalesce(w.buckets, 0) AS buckets_in_window,
  to_timestamp(l.last_bucket) AS latest_bucket,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_bucket)::bigint AS age_secs,
  round(
    (extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_bucket) / l.granularity_secs, 1
  ) AS age_cadences
FROM lifetime AS l
LEFT JOIN windowed AS w
  ON
    l.source = w.source
    AND l.product_id = w.product_id
    AND l.granularity_secs = w.granularity_secs
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

panels.title: Candle coverage (all time, window ${coverage_mins} min)

panels.description:
Which venues are printing which products into the tick tier, and how fresh each is. A tick row has neither a bucket width nor OHLCV, which is why this tier is a separate table from the candle coverage above rather than merged into it.

AGE IS COUNTED IN EXPECTED INTERVALS, not seconds, and that is the colored column. Three of the five tick sources publish once a day, so the 60/180-second bounds this panel used to carry marked er-api and Frankfurter red whenever they were perfectly healthy — measured at about 83,000 seconds old, which is just what a daily reference looks like. The expected interval is declared per source, because nothing in the store records a source's cadence and every version derived from the readings was suppressed by the outage it had to report.

A source that published nothing inside the window has NO ROW here at all. Source coverage above accounts for all eight sources by name whatever they have done, and is the panel to read for an absence rather than this one.

targets.rawSql:
-- Which venues are printing which products into the tick tier, and how fresh.
--
-- AGE IS COUNTED IN EXPECTED INTERVALS for the same reason the candle table
-- counts buckets: three of the five tick sources publish once a day, so the
-- 60/180-second bounds this panel used to carry marked er-api and Frankfurter
-- red whenever they were perfectly healthy -- measured at roughly 83,000
-- seconds old, which is simply what a daily reference looks like. The expected
-- interval is declared per source because nothing in the store records a
-- source's cadence, and every form derived from the readings themselves is
-- suppressed by the outage it would have to report.
--
-- Note the window: a source that published nothing inside it has no row here
-- at all. Source coverage renders every source by name whatever it has done,
-- and is the panel to read for an absence.
WITH cadence AS (
  SELECT
    d.source,
    d.expected_secs
  FROM (VALUES
    ('coinbase', 60),
    ('kraken', 60),
    ('erapi', 86400),
    ('frankfurter', 86400),
    ('pyth', 60)
  ) AS d (source, expected_secs)
)

SELECT
  s.source,
  s.product_id,
  count(*) AS prints,
  to_timestamp(max(s.observed_at)) AS latest_print,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(s.observed_at))::bigint AS age_secs,
  round(
    (extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(s.observed_at))
    / coalesce(d.expected_secs, 60), 1
  ) AS age_intervals
FROM spot_ticks AS s
LEFT JOIN cadence AS d ON s.source = d.source
WHERE
  s.observed_at
  >= extract(epoch FROM now()) - (${coverage_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60)
GROUP BY s.source, s.product_id, d.expected_secs
ORDER BY 1, 2

panels.title: Tick coverage (last ${coverage_mins} min)

panels.description:
Is each source still landing rows at its expected rate, and did it stop mid-window. Shape over time exists nowhere else on this dashboard, and dating the onset of an outage is a real forensic need.

A DEAD COLLECTOR IS A FLAT LINE AT ZERO, not a missing series. That is the point of the redesign: grouping over the measurement table alone drops a source that wrote nothing for the whole window, so the panel looked TIDIER the longer an outage ran, and the reader's eye had to notice an absence rather than a change. Every source that has ever written this product and bucket width is seeded across the window, so an outage now adds ink. The series are LINES and are deliberately NOT stacked, which is what makes that literally true: a stacked bar of height zero draws no pixels at all, so under the obvious form a dead collector would still have been invisible on the chart and present only in the legend.

Expected means "has ever written this shape", not "is in the registry" — all-time history cannot be erased by an outage, and it also avoids drawing a permanent zero line for a tick-only source that has never written a candle. A source that legitimately publishes once a day will sit at zero between publications; read it against the Role column of Source coverage rather than as an outage.

Counts are candle ROWS per minute across the selected products, so a source covering four products at 60s tops out around four.

targets.rawSql:
-- Is each source still landing rows at its expected rate, and did it stop
-- mid-window. The CTE is load-bearing, not style: Grafana captures macro
-- arguments with a regex that stops at the first closing paren, so wrapping
-- the epoch column in a to_timestamp call inside the time-group macro leaves
-- it one truncated argument and the query fails to interpolate. Converting the
-- column in a CTE first hands the macro a bare column name, which is all it
-- can parse. For the same reason, do not name a macro in a comment here: the
-- scanner does not skip comments and will try to interpolate the example.
--
-- EVERY EXPECTED SOURCE IS SEEDED AT BOTH ENDS OF THE WINDOW, which is the
-- whole redesign. Grouping over the measurement table alone omits a series
-- ENTIRELY for a collector that was dead the whole window, so the panel got
-- cleaner as an outage lengthened and an outage removed ink instead of adding
-- it. Two zero rows per expected source cost nothing, guarantee the series
-- exists, and let the time-group fill draw it flat across the range: a dead
-- collector is now a line pinned at zero. The panel draws unstacked LINES for
-- that last clause to be true -- a stacked bar of height zero renders nothing,
-- which would have left the seeded series visible only in the legend.
--
-- EXPECTED MEANS "HAS EVER WRITTEN THIS SHAPE", deliberately not "is in the
-- registry". All-time history cannot be suppressed by an outage of any
-- length, so it is fail-closed, while it also declines to invent a permanent
-- zero line for a tick-only source that never wrote a candle in its life.
WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT
    $__unixEpochFrom() AS lo,
    $__unixEpochTo() AS hi
),

expected AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT c.source
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  WHERE c.source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND c.granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
),

seeded AS (
  SELECT
    to_timestamp(b.lo) AS bucket_ts,
    e.source,
    0 AS written
  FROM expected AS e
  CROSS JOIN bounds AS b
  UNION ALL
  SELECT
    to_timestamp(b.hi) AS bucket_ts,
    e.source,
    0 AS written
  FROM expected AS e
  CROSS JOIN bounds AS b
  UNION ALL
  SELECT
    to_timestamp(c.bucket_start) AS bucket_ts,
    c.source,
    1 AS written
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(c.bucket_start)
    AND c.source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND c.granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
)

SELECT
  $__timeGroupAlias(bucket_ts, '1m', 0),
  source AS metric,
  sum(written) AS value
FROM seeded
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Candle rows per minute by source

panels.description:
Did a collector keep polling while storing nothing. Every store-sink batch now records how many records it offered and how many rows it actually wrote, so attrition that previously left only a debug log line is visible here.

READ A RUN, NOT A ROW. A polling collector legitimately offers an empty batch whenever the venue has not published the next bucket yet, so a non-zero empty_intake count is normal and is NOT a fault on its own. The reportable state is a feed whose stored count is zero across the whole window while its market is open, which is what the ordering surfaces first.

ALL_DUPLICATE IS NOT ATTRITION, and separating it is the point of the table. Delivery is at-least-once, so after a crash-restart a resumed window re-offers records the writer already holds and every one dedups away. Those batches wrote zero rows and are working exactly as designed — a detector keyed on "wrote nothing" would flag them, which is why they are counted apart from empty_intake rather than with it. That exemption is per BATCH, not per window: a feed whose whole window is all_duplicate has stored nothing new the entire time and is stuck re-fetching, so it has stored = 0 and DOES sort to the top, correctly.

ABSENCE IS AMBIGUOUS HERE — READ IT WITH CARE. This records batches that happened, so a feed with no row in the window is not necessarily healthy and not necessarily parked. At least four states render as the same absence: a source parked by decision; a collector that is not running; a collector whose batch ERRORED, since the counts are recorded inside the batch transaction and an error aborts it before the row is written; and a feed whose poll interval is longer than the selected window, or which stopped before the window opened. The silent-feed-first ordering can only rank a feed that has at least one row in range, so a feed that vanishes entirely will NOT sort to the top. Cross-read against Collector cursor age and Source coverage, which render every declared source by name whatever it has done.

targets.rawSql:
-- Did a collector keep polling while storing nothing. Each store-sink batch
-- records the records it offered and the rows it actually wrote, so attrition
-- that used to leave only a debug log line is durable and readable here.
--
-- READ A RUN, NOT A ROW. A polling collector legitimately offers an empty
-- batch whenever the venue has not published the next bucket yet, so a
-- non-zero empty_intake count is ordinary. The reportable state is a feed
-- whose stored count is zero for the whole window while its market is open,
-- which is what the ordering below puts at the top.
--
-- ALL_DUPLICATE IS NOT ATTRITION. Delivery is at-least-once, so a resumed
-- window re-offers records the writer already holds and every one dedups
-- away. Those batches wrote zero rows and are behaving exactly as designed,
-- which is why they are counted apart from empty_intake rather than with it.
-- The exemption is per BATCH: a window that is ENTIRELY all_duplicate stored
-- nothing new throughout, so it has stored = 0 and sorts to the top, correctly.
--
-- The aggregate is repeated in the ORDER BY rather than reusing the output
-- name: Postgres exposes an output column name to ORDER BY only as a bare
-- name, not inside an expression, so the alias would resolve against the
-- table and fail.
--
-- ABSENCE IS AMBIGUOUS. This records batches that happened, so a feed with no
-- row in the window may be parked by decision, not running, erroring before the
-- row is written (the counts share the batch transaction), or simply polling
-- more slowly than the window. The ordering below can only rank a feed that has
-- a row in range, so one that vanishes does NOT sort to the top -- cross-read
-- Collector cursor age and Source coverage, which name every source regardless.
SELECT
  feed,
  count(*) AS batches,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'stored') AS stored,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'all_duplicate') AS all_duplicate,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'empty_intake') AS empty_intake,
  sum(requested) AS rows_requested,
  sum(written) AS rows_written,
  max(observed_at) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'stored') AS last_stored
FROM feed_batch_ingestion
WHERE $__timeFilter(observed_at)
GROUP BY feed
ORDER BY (count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'stored') = 0) DESC, feed

panels.title: Batch ingestion by feed (did a collector store nothing)

panels.description:
Do two venues quoting the same pair agree, and does anything move between candle closes. The tick half is what makes this panel move between closes: 60s is the finest bucket any candle endpoint offers, so the candle half cannot show intra-minute movement however often it is polled.

THE ROSTER IS NOT A FLAT POOL, and the line styling says so. A designated TAPE is drawn thick — OANDA on an FX pair, Coinbase or Kraken on a crypto or peg leg; the intraday margin source is drawn solid and thin; the DAILY REFERENCES — Alpha Vantage, er-api and Frankfurter — are dotted, because their divergence from the tape is their nature rather than a fault. Three of the five FX sources are daily, so a dotted line sitting at a different level is not a reason to pull anything; a THICK line diverging from the others is.

That marking is a DESIGNATION carried in this panel's styling, and the same designation is carried as a Role column by Source coverage. Nothing in the store records it, so the two must be kept in step by hand until a collector-written cadence column exists.

The candle arm filters on bucket size and the tick arm cannot, since a tick has no bucket width. The granularity picker is now driven from the data, so it can no longer offer a bucket size the selected sources do not write — which is what used to make the candle arm vanish while the tick arm kept drawing, with nothing on the panel to say why.

targets.rawSql:
-- Candle closes and spot ticks in one series set. The tick half is
-- what makes this panel move BETWEEN candle closes: 60s is the finest
-- bucket any candle endpoint offers, so the candle half cannot show
-- intra-minute movement however often it is polled.
--
-- Tick series are suffixed so the legend distinguishes them from the
-- same venue's candle series, and they carry no granularity filter
-- because a tick has no bucket width.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS "time",
  source || ' ' || product_id AS metric,
  "close" AS value
FROM cex_prices
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
UNION ALL
SELECT
  to_timestamp(observed_at) AS "time",
  source || ' ' || product_id || ' tick' AS metric,
  price AS value
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(observed_at)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Price by source

panels.description:
Do the recorded candles look like a real market — the price-shape read, kept on the dashboard a bring-up reader actually opens.

The dashboard's default range is two days, which is wide enough to show a session's shape at 60s buckets and to hold two prints of a daily reference. It used to be fifteen minutes, which drew FIFTEEN BARS and made the panel read as broken rather than as narrow. For deeper history use the All data link at the top, which starts the range at this selection's own first collected bar; there is no time-picker preset that can know when collection started, and any relative window wide enough to hold the whole series also pads the chart with dead space.

One panel per product, so the source and product pickers must stay paired: this panel draws a single candle source, and a source carrying none of the selected products paints nothing.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS "time",
  "open",
  "high",
  "low",
  "close",
  "volume"
FROM cex_prices
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
  AND source = ${candle_source:sqlstring}
  AND product_id = ${product_id:sqlstring}
  AND granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
ORDER BY bucket_start

panels.title: OHLC ${product_id} (${candle_source}, ${granularity}s buckets)

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT asset_class FROM instruments ORDER BY 1
list.description: Asset class, which NARROWS THE PRODUCT PICKER below it rather than filtering any panel directly. Nothing reads this variable except the product query, so changing it changes which products are offerable and nothing else — if a product you expect is missing from that picker, this is why.
list.label: Class
list.name: class
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT asset_class FROM instruments ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT product_id FROM instruments WHERE asset_class = ANY (ARRAY[${class:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1
list.description: Every product any collector is configured to poll, from the instruments dimension, narrowed to the selected Class. Registry-driven rather than a scan of the measurement tables, which matters three ways: it covers both tiers by construction - most of the roster is tick-only, since only EURC reaches a CEX candle endpoint - a newly added pair appears before its first row lands, and it costs one small-table read instead of a DISTINCT over two unbounded tables on every dashboard load. The class filter uses the sqlstring formatter inside an ARRAY, not a regex inside a quoted literal: the regex formatter does not escape quotes, and ARRAY[] stays valid SQL when nothing is selected where IN () is a syntax error. Defaults to the three MVP FX pairs rather than All, and that default is load-bearing rather than taste: the OHLC panel repeats over this variable at full width, so All renders one full-width chart per instrument. At 33 instruments that is 33 stacked charts pushing roughly 330 grid rows between the top of the dashboard and everything under it - including Tick coverage and Source coverage, which are the only two panels where a tick-only venue such as Kraken appears at all. Most of those charts are also empty, since the default candle source carries candles for a single product. Drill-down is unaffected: the drop-down still offers every product and All.
list.label: Product
list.name: product_id
list.query: SELECT product_id FROM instruments WHERE asset_class = ANY (ARRAY[${class:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM instrument_registry ORDER BY 1
list.description: Sources from both tiers, so the tick-only venues (kraken, pyth, erapi, frankfurter) are selectable rather than absent. Note that 'coinbase' appears once but writes both tiers - the table a row lives in is what distinguishes a print from a bucket, not the source label.
list.label: Source
list.name: source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM instrument_registry ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM cex_prices ORDER BY 1
list.description:
The single source the candlestick panel draws. Candles from two venues cannot share one set of bars.

This default is paired with the Product default and must stay paired: the panel filters on BOTH, so a source carrying none of the defaulted products paints nothing at all. oanda carries all three MVP anchors — EUR-USD, AUD-USD and CAD-USD — so the panel paints on first load; coinbase, the previous default, carries candles for EURC-USDC alone and would leave every repeat empty.

CAD-USD renders on this dashboard: it joined the keyed roster and three sources now write its candles, two of them intraday. So an empty CAD-USD panel is a fault to chase, not an expected state.
list.label: Candle source
list.name: candle_source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM cex_prices ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT c.granularity_secs FROM cex_prices AS c WHERE c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[]) AND (c.source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[]) OR c.source = ${candle_source:sqlstring}) ORDER BY 1
list.description:
Bucket size, in seconds, listing only the values the current selection actually holds. Query-driven rather than a fixed list, and the change is a bug fix: the fixed list offered all six bucket sizes the schema permits while only two have ever had rows, and validity is paired to the source — the candle venues write 60s buckets and the daily-only FX vendor writes 86400s ones — so four of six selections blanked four panels, two of them liveness readings, and a blank panel is indistinguishable from a broken one. The sibling FX dashboard already drove granularity from its source and product; this is the same fix, filtered on the product and on either source picker so a value is offered only if some selected source can render it.

On a cold database this variable is EMPTY, which is the honest signal that nothing has been collected yet and is strictly better than offering a choice that renders nothing. That is what forces the guard every consumer here carries: the filters compare it as TEXT. An empty expansion of a bare numeric reference is a SQL parse error rather than an empty result, and a parse error fails before any row is considered — so this panel set used to hardcode the list precisely to avoid that. The trade is now taken deliberately and paid for, rather than avoided by offering dead values.

Excluded from URL sync, unlike the pickers above it: a bucket size pinned in a shared or reloaded link can outlive the selection it was valid for and then silently blank every panel. Treat it as derived from the source and product pickers rather than as state of its own.

ONE KNOWN BOUND on the scope: a value is offered if EITHER source picker can render it, because this one variable serves panels that filter on Source and the candlestick that filters on Candle source, and no single scope satisfies both — the union over-offers, the intersection can be empty. So with Candle source on a daily vendor and Source on an intraday one, 86400 is offerable and the throughput panel will draw nothing. That is narrower than the defect this replaced (four of six values blanking four panels) and it is operator-driven rather than silent, but it is not zero.
list.label: Granularity
list.name: granularity
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT c.granularity_secs FROM cex_prices AS c WHERE c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[]) AND (c.source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[]) OR c.source = ${candle_source:sqlstring}) ORDER BY 1

list.description: The coverage table's window, in minutes. Independent of the dashboard time range on purpose: 'what is arriving now' should not change when you pan back to look at history. URL sync is off, like the freshness bound's: a window silently adopted from a shared or stale link fails in the OPEN direction, because a wide window keeps counting buckets for a source that stopped hours ago and so reads as if it were still arriving.
list.label: Coverage window (min)
list.name: coverage_mins

list.description:
How recent the designated tape's newest reading must be to count as printing right now. This is the go/no-go panel's whole liveness test, and it is also the bound behind Source coverage's Printing now column — two panels, one picker, which is worth knowing before you move it, and there is deliberately no cadence classifier beside it — an earlier version had one and it failed open, reclassifying a long-dead intraday venue as a daily source.

TREAT THIS AS THE HALT'S DETECTION LATENCY, not as a display preference: it is how long the tape may go quiet before the pair reads no-go. The default of 15 is not arbitrary — it mirrors the maker's own per-leg tape staleness bound, so the panel goes red no later than the engine refuses the leg.

THE LIST IS CAPPED AT THE BOUND, so this picker can only ever tighten the test, never loosen it. It previously reached 1440 minutes — 96 times the maker's tape bound — at which a day-dead tape scored as quotable, which is failing open in exactly the ruled-against direction. The old argument for offering it was that a picker value is chosen deliberately and stays visible while a URL value is adopted silently; that distinction is real but it does not make a fail-open reading safe to offer, and the operator ruled the cap in. Reading history over a wider window is the coverage tables' job, and they carry their own window that is independent of this one.

The one thing no setting can do is let a daily reference clear the halt, since only the designated tape reaches the tape column. URL sync is deliberately off, so a stale shared link cannot pin a value here.
list.label: Minimum quotable freshness (min)
list.name: quote_freshness_mins

list.definition: SELECT min(c.bucket_start) * 1000 FROM cex_prices AS c WHERE c.source = ${candle_source:sqlstring} AND c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[]) AND c.granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
list.description: The epoch-millisecond timestamp of the earliest collected bar for the candlestick's current selection. Hidden, and not a control: it exists so the All data link can widen the time range to exactly where this series starts rather than to a fixed relative window, which would pad the chart with empty space that grows by a day every day. The link ends at now rather than at the last collected bar, so a series that has stopped still shows the gap between its final bar and the present — the only on-chart signal that it is dead. Known soft edge: an aggregate with no grouping returns one null row rather than no rows, so on a selection holding nothing this expands to an empty range bound and the link degrades to resetting the time picker with no indication it did.
list.label: Data start
list.name: data_from
list.query: SELECT min(c.bucket_start) * 1000 FROM cex_prices AS c WHERE c.source = ${candle_source:sqlstring} AND c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[]) AND c.granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}

title: Market data
